text.p: These are the main stories in Latvian newspapers on Wednesday. Prepared for Reuters by the Cooperation Fund. Reuters has not verified these reports and does not vouch for their accuracy:
- Prime Minister Andris Shkele met pupils of a secondary school who took part in international contests and gained 11 bronze medals and two honorary diplomas.

- General Prosecutor Janis Skrastinsh announced that his office has finalised the official accusation against Alexandr Lavent, former chairman of the collapsed Banka Baltiya. Skrastinsh believes the court will not start considering the case before February 1997.

- Several hundred people held a rally at Grizinkalns in Riga to commemorate the fifth anniversary of the Latvian parliament's laws on citizenship, which those without citizenship, mainly Russian-speakers, say deprived them of their rights.
- The government approved amendments to the law on Local councils which envisage liquidation of elected authorities at the district level.
- The government is working on plans to reduce the tax-exempted minimum wage, which is now 25 lats, to bridge a 12 million lats gap in next year's budget.
- A working group consisting of experts from the defence and foreign ministries met President Guntis Ulmanis before leaving for Brussels to take part in a third round of talks with NATO.

- The leaders of the three major ruling parties, Democratic Party Saimnieks, Latvia's Way and Fatherland and Freedom, are reported to have met at the end of last week to discuss possible scenarios on changing the government.
- The police say an explosion in one of Riga's sports halls on October 14 was an attempt on the life of a man alleged to have links with organised crime.
- The government will revoke the weapons contract with Slovak company Katrim Stella, which allegedly supplied Latvia with defective infantry weapons, made in the CIS.
- Riga city council voted to take a $5 million loan from the Ministry of Finance.

- The U.S. Export and Import Bank has agreed to guarantee a $6.7 million loan to Latvian Railroads from the Bank of New York for the purchase of telecommunications equipment, thus concluding its first deal with Latvia.
